modal recursion, reinterpreting it through the lens of advanced programming
theories that incorporate sophisticated concepts like monadic polymorphic
recursion schemes and modal operators within denotational frameworks. This
paper takes a different perspective, focusing on the relationship between
programming languages and combinatory logic. By introducing a basic
combinatory extension that enables expressions to manipulate variable names,
we establish a strong connection between this extension and modal recursion,
showing that any program expressible in the latter can also be expressed in
the former. Furthermore, we define a fundamental programming language grounded
in combinatory logic, which serves as the basis for several related systems.
This foundational language forms the core of SPC, a family of programming
theories that incorporates various programming languages with explicit name
management. SPC encompasses a range of languages with explicit name operations,
including a variant of Wadler's namesplate proposal, as well as two other
subsystems. SPC's framework allows for a hierarchy of theories, enabling
the seamless integration of multiple languages and their name-related abstractions.
This hierarchical structure facilitates the creation of a unified name management
framework, which can be used across multiple languages in a coherent and
consistent manner. As part of the formal framework, SPC includes a general
theory of explicit names, which serves as the foundation for various language
instantiations, including the combinatorial extension and its associated
combinatory logic. This names-based framework provides a strong foundation for
the development of programming theories focused on explicit name management. 
As such, it is expected to play a central role in the ongoing SPC research initiative.

In particular, our analysis highlights that vectorization is crucial for achieving high performance, with even simple non-vectorized code producing slow results; this underlines the importance of choosing the right tools for numerical computing. Our analysis also highlights that numerical computing performance is highly dependent on the specific tasks being performed, underscoring the need for thorough benchmarking before selecting a library for real-world use. Furthermore, our study reveals that numerical performance does not always correlate with language performance; this suggests that existing general-purpose programming languages may be viable options for high-performance numerical computing, particularly when paired with specialized libraries. This research also explores the feasibility of automatically vectorizing non-vector code using static code analysis and rewriting, demonstrating that this approach can be both efficient and effective; this technique is illustrated through the optimization of the Apache Commons Math library. Our study ultimately concludes that numerical computing libraries for general-purpose programming languages are becoming increasingly efficient and effective, thanks to advances in compiler technology and automatic vectorization. As such, physicists can now enjoy high-performance numerical computing without needing to resort to specialized languages like Fortran, C, or C++. In this study, we develop a new approach to detect social bias in large, detailed datasets that include extensive information on individual characteristics. Our method, which focuses on groups that didn't exist in traditional fairness frameworks, effectively identifies and quantifies social bias in these multi-faceted datasets. Utilizing a unique representation of the dataset, our approach breaks it down into distinct sub-groups based on their inherent characteristics and measures bias using a modified version of the Maximum Mean Discrepancy. To verify the effectiveness of our approach, we apply it to a large collection of university policies and a comprehensive dataset of online job postings, revealing significant social bias in both cases. Our findings not only highlight the presence of previously unrecognized forms of social bias but also underscore the importance of considering the intricate interplay of different identity categories. $\gamma$ radiation is a significant concern for the precision experiments that search for beyond Standard Model signs, as it can cause contamination more severe than the background from cosmic radiation. We conducted a study of the low energy background near the mass-5 laboratory in Mainz, Germany, to better understand the sources of the background near these experiments. We measured the activity of radon in the air and the radioactivity associated with 222Rn's decay products on the surface and underground, as well as the radioactivity of 210Pb, 212Bi, and 212Po. We found that the levels of cosmic background in the underground laboratory were about 1-2 orders of magnitude lower than the surface levels, and the dominant source of the background was indeed radon and its decay products. We further analyzed the data to develop a model that describes the activity of 222Rn in terms of location, depth, and time of the year, which can be used to estimate the background near similar experiments. This model can be applied to any depth and location with minimal adjustments for the local geology and the specific characteristics of the site. We also found that the background from the decay of naturally occurring radionuclies like 210Bi and 210Po was significant at the laboratory level, and we proposed a method to remove their influence on the background measurement. This method, however, is not applicable underground due to the low levels of activity. We further investigated the low energy background at the laboratory by measuring the activity of 214Bi and 214Po, as well as the radioactivity of 226Ra, which is the decay product of 222Rn. We found that the activity of 214Bi and 214Po was about 1-2 orders of magnitude lower than the surface levels, and the dominant source of the background was indeed the radioactivity of 226Ra. We further analyzed the data to develop a model that describes the activity of 226Ra in terms of location, depth, and time of the year, which can be used to estimate the background near similar experiments. This process is essential in several fields, such as image analysis, where different objects can be naturally grouped. By training a classifier on noise-tolerant features, RLS is able to uncover the core patterns in a dataset that are resilient to noise. Our method is evaluated using real-world datasets, and the results demonstrate its effectiveness in finding the core patterns in a dataset. Let $N$ be the size of $S$, and let $K$ be a lower bound for the smallest non-zero sum of variables in $S$. To explore this, we examine the experiences of three online game communities that shifted from proprietary to open-source models. Our goal is to identify the benefits and challenges associated with this transition and to understand the strategies that can facilitate or hinder this process. 
  Methodology: Through a mixed-methods approach combining surveys, interviews, and focus groups, we studied the community-driven development of three open-source games: FreeCAD, Inkscape, and Tux Paint. Our research involved gathering data from various sources, including 52 in-depth interviews with key individuals, 246 survey responses, and 8 focus group sessions across the three communities. 
  Findings: Our analysis suggests that open-source communities benefit from increased transparency, trust, and social connections among members. However, open-source models can also lead to conflicts within communities, create power imbalances among contributors, and create difficulties in managing expectations around involvement. 
  Conclusions: Our research indicates that open-source models can be successful in software development but may not be the best fit for all types of creative projects. To ensure a smooth transition to open-source models, project leaders should prioritize building strong relationships within communities and establish clear expectations around involvement. Open-source models can also present opportunities for community members to take on leadership roles and become leaders within their respective projects. 
  Recommendations: Our research offers several recommendations for project leaders considering the open-source model, including fostering a sense of community, being transparent about decision-making processes, and creating clear expectations around involvement. Additionally, our research highlights the importance of community leaders in facilitating open-source transitions and suggests that project leaders should prioritize building strong relationships within their respective communities. 
  Future Research: Our research leaves several unanswered questions, particularly regarding the long-term impact of open-source models on community dynamics and the role of leadership within these ecosystems. Future research could investigate these topics in more depth, potentially exploring the experiences of open-source game communities over extended periods of time. Future research could also delve into the role of leadership within these ecosystems, potentially examining the ways in which community leaders facilitate open-source transitions and maintain community cohesion.

Our approach leverages the equivalent reformulation of these problems as linear decision problems, where the cost is taken as minimum rather than average. This formulation's optimality is confirmed by the existence of worst-case or average-case transportation plans. To efficiently solve this linear decision problem, we adapt a dynamic programming strategy, originally developed for the partial order problem. This approach is complemented by a probabilistic principle, originally derived for the Bonferroni mean, that enables us to calculate the minimum cost corresponding to an extreme probability measure. As a result, we can solve the Wasserstein and universal transportation problems in $O(n \log n)$ time, where $n$ is the number of points in the finite set. This allows us to efficiently compute these distances for any probability measure on a large finite set of points in near-linear time. Moreover, our approach generalizes to other problems involving partial orderings, and we demonstrate its application in computing the Gare-Wets graph and the shortest path metric induced by the partial order. Additionally, we investigate the computational complexity of approximating these problems exactly. Our findings indicate that approximating these problems in polynomial time is NP-hard, and even approximating them up to a constant factor is NP-hard, even when allowing for randomness. However, we also find that approximating these problems with a factor greater than 1/2 is NP-hard, and we identify a reduction from the 3-partition problem that approximates the problems with a factor of at most $1/\sqrt{2}$, and is at least as hard as the 3-partition problem. This suggests that achieving a better approximation factor is NP-hard, and may be unfeasible. We have developed a theoretical model for an interacting Bose-Hubbard system, accounting for both single- and two-body interactions, to study the evolution of the excitonic order parameter. However, the presence of eye movements causes adjacent pixels to move into each other's positions, distorting the appearance of individual red blood cells and creating artifacts on angiography images. This study investigates the impact of eye movements on OCTA images by analyzing the movement patterns of pixels in a dataset consisting of 22 patient scans. It also demonstrates that by applying a 2D Gaussian filter, the effects of eye movements can be minimized, resulting in improved numerical values for the structural correlation parameter (ρ) and the effective integration time (A_{eff}). The optimal Gaussian kernel size for mitigating eye movements was found to be 3-5 pixels, with a corresponding decrease in the variance of ρ by 70% and the variance of A_{eff} by 75%. Furthermore, the presence of neighboring vessels also affects the integration time, with a suggested method for mitigating its influence. By applying this method, the effects of neighboring vessels on A_{eff} can be minimized, reducing its variance by 85-95%. The optimal Gaussian kernel size for mitigating eye movements was found to be 3-5 pixels, with a corresponding decrease in the variance of A_{eff} by 75% and the variance of ρ by 70%. This research provides a new approach for improving the quantification of capillary density and the structural correlation parameter in OCTA imaging. It also has the potential to enhance the accuracy of OCTA-derived metrics in assessing retinal and choroidal vascular diseases. The proposed method can be incorporated into existing OCTA imaging software to automatically mitigate eye movements and neighboring vessels, ultimately leading to more reliable eye health diagnoses. speakers in spoken dialogue is essential for various applications like audio-visual speech recognition and speaker diarization. Current methods often rely on pre-trained object detectors and estimate speaker positions based on the locations of the detected objects. However, these approaches can be flawed as they may not accurately capture the complex temporal relationships between consecutive speaker events. To address this limitation, we propose a novel temporal speaker detection network that leverages pre-trained models and models their temporal aspects by representing dialogue segments as alternating speaker patterns. Our approach is evaluated on the newly created SpeakerLocation dataset and achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods. Notably, our method demonstrates a 0.07 meters mean average error reduction. The dataset and code are publicly available. Additionally, the package offers tools to calculate rotation periods based on Doppler shift measurements, as well as tools to map the distribution of angular momentum in binary systems and extrasolar planets, and to compute the rotation rate of fluid planets using both the precession and spin limits. Furthermore, \textbf{GalRotpy} includes a sub-module for calculating rotating frame effects on planetary atmospheres, specifically due to the combined influences of the planet's spin and its parent star's gravitational force. This module employs the streamlines method to visualize the rotating frame effects on atmospheric gas movement. \textbf{GalRotpy} offers extensive documentation, including detailed guides, example use cases, and doctest-based documentation, as well as a comprehensive tutorial for users to gain hands-on experience with the library.   Although deep learning and formal verification share the goal of ensuring system reliability,

  Coq to illustrate the different methodologies employed in each area. 

  The first part will introduce formal verification techniques for deep learning, which are still in their early stages. 
  These techniques primarily draw on functional programming and category theory. 

  The second part will focus on formal verification techniques for self-driving cars, which primarily rely on real algebraic geometry and state space modeling. 

  The third part will cover the outcomes of the DeepSpec project, which aimed to develop formal verification techniques for deep learning. 
  Although the project achieved significant advancements, it encountered substantial technical hurdles and limitations. 
  These obstacles and limitations will be examined in detail. 

  The fourth part will conclude the lectures with a discussion of potential future research directions in formal verification for deep learning. 
  These potential research directions will be highlighted using concrete examples and illustrated using Coq. 

  The lectures will cover multiple approaches to formal verification, which is why we will also explore other methodologies,

To address this challenge, researchers have developed multiple methods for stabilizing the GAN training process. However, a major limitation of existing methods is that they fail to provide clear insights into why GAN training is difficult. To overcome this limitation, a new approach, called SPGAN, is proposed in this research. SPGAN combines two advanced GAN training techniques: geometric deep learning based activation weight optimization in the discriminator and a self-training strategy with virtual adversarial learning in the generator. SPGAN is a simple yet powerful approach that provides clear and intuitive explanations for stabilizing the GAN training process. Through comprehensive experiments, it is demonstrated that SPGAN achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple datasets, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, STL-10, LSUN-church, and CelebA, while also matching the performance of leading competitors in unsupervised image-to-image translation tasks. Notably, the generator in SPGAN produces high-quality samples that are comparable to those produced by the GAN baseline. To facilitate future research, the code and models for SPGAN are made publicly available. SPGAN achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on the unsupervised image-to-image translation task on the LSUN-church dataset. To further validate the effectiveness of SPGAN, the approach is applied to a variety of challenging computer vision applications, including super-resolution, de-noising, de-mosaicing, de-blurring, and facial recognition. The results show that SPGAN achieves a new state-of-the-art performance on the unsupervised image-to-image translation task on the LSUN-church dataset, while also matching the performance of leading competitors in the other applications. To the best of our knowledge, the work on facial recognition using SPGAN is the first of its kind in the literature. When faced with hidden relationships between nodes that cannot be directly accessed, GNN struggles to effectively learn from these constraints. To address this limitation, we propose a novel GNN architecture called edge-tensor GNN (eTensorGNN), which aims to directly capture the latent relationships between nodes via an edge tensor. Theoretical analysis and empirical evaluations confirm the enhanced performance of eTensorGNN in capturing graph structure, resulting in superior performance across multiple real-world datasets. In many contexts, it is necessary to employ batch MCMC, which generates sets of independent samples due to unexpected events, system crashes, or the simple termination of a program. Although state recovery is often possible for some batch MCMC methods, this capability is not universally available. Consequently, selecting the optimal number of iterations and mixtures to guarantee approximate posterior distributions is a challenging task. This paper presents a straightforward, non-intrusive approach for assessing the similarity between approximate posterior distributions produced by batch MCMC and the actual posterior distributions. This method is based on the Riemannian Wasserstein distance and is applied to three real-world datasets. Notably, the proposed technique is non-intrusive, meaning it doesn't require access to the internal workings of the employed MCMC code. Instead, it relies solely on the generated samples and a proposal distribution. The results demonstrate that the proposed method is effective, efficient, and easy to use. Ultimately, the goal of this work is to provide a reliable tool for assessing the quality of inference methods. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/alexandremenendez/wasser_mcmc. The code enables users to run the experiments described in this paper, including visualizing the results. Moreover, the provided code serves as a flexible tool for exploring the properties of various MCMC algorithms in batch settings. This flexibility allows users to easily adapt the code to evaluate the performance of their preferred MCMC implementations. The code's main functionality is to compute the empirical Riemannian Wasserstein distance for a given set of samples. This value represents the maximum distance between two probability measures. The code also includes a function to estimate this distance empirically, given a reference probability measure and a set of samples. The main contribution of this work is to demonstrate that the Riemannian Wasserstein distance can effectively distinguish between accurate and inaccurate posterior approximations produced by MCMC methods. The experiments conducted in this study are designed to test the ability of the proposed method to distinguish between correct and incorrect posterior distributions. The results show that the proposed approach is effective in detecting incorrect posterior distributions while producing minimal false positives. The experiments also reveal that the proposed method is capable of distinguishing between correct posterior distributions with high accuracy. The results of this study suggest that the Riemannian Wasserstein distance can be used as a reliable metric for evaluating the quality of MCMC methods in batch settings. The

Notably, it is shown that bagging can fail dramatically when trained on noisy labels - in the sense that its performance can be no better than random guessing and can even be worse. This unexpected finding challenges the conventional understanding that bagging always improves model accuracy. Furthermore, a new method of regularized bagging (RB) for addressing noisy labels is proposed, and our theoretical findings demonstrate that it can successfully learn from noisy labels with high accuracy. Experimental results corroborate our theoretical predictions and highlight the importance of our analysis. This research offers the first comprehensive theoretical examination of bagging for learning from noisy labels. Additionally, our study of RB provides valuable insights for future research on learning from noisy labels. The accompanying code can be found at https://github.com/chenziwei2020/Bagging. to a typical e-commerce website, offering users with the most relevant products from numerous sellers. The ranking of search results affects users' preferences and ultimately influences sales. However, determining the optimal result order poses a difficulty due to conflicting interests between different sellers, each seeking higher visibility. To address this challenge, we propose a novel ranking approach, SellerRank, which incorporates users' behavior into seller-centric ranking. By leveraging the potential of deep learning, SellerRank accurately predicts the potential of each seller based on the embedded seller features and top-bucket seller embeddings. The evaluation demonstrates that SellerRank yields a 12.9% increase in sales and a 10.9% decrease in click fraud rate compared to the baseline. Moreover, it also reduces dependency on third-party verification services specializing in e-commerce click filtering. The implementation of SellerRank using TensorFlow showcases its feasibility with modern e-commerce infrastructure. The application of SellerRank on an actual e-commerce platform verifies its practicality. The source code is available at https://github.com/anhnguyen95/SellerRank. This paper explores the potential of combining domain decomposition and time-space finite difference methods using artificial neural networks to approximate solutions to the Allen-Cahn equation. We implement this approach in one and two dimensions with multiple sub-domains, considering both periodic and non-periodic boundary conditions. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we tested it with exact solutions to the equation. We observed that our approach yields accurate results that depend on the number of grid points, sub-domains, and hidden layers in our networks. This method is simple to implement and does not require extensive training. We also investigated the impact of various parameters on our results. Our numerical experiments show that our approach converges at a rate of $C^2$ in space and $C^1$ in time. This method can be extended to other partial differential equations and may be influenced by other factors such as the geometry of the sub-domains. However, this aspect requires further investigation. We also found that our approach can accurately capture the global minimum energy level in the two-dimensional Allen-Cann equation with Neumann boundary conditions. In models featuring multiple scalar fields within the Standard Model, especially those including a lepton field, due to the reduced binding energy required for Q-ball formation, a lower formation energy threshold applies.  As a result, even when quantum fluctuations exceed this threshold, multi-field Q-balls can still form effortlessly.  In contrast, single-field Q-balls need to surpass a higher threshold to form. In the context of the seesaw mechanism for generating small neutrino masses, multi-field Q-balls emerge as a natural solution, and the formation of these Q-balls is even facilitated when the lepton fields undergo spontaneous symmetry breaking. In this context, our study examines the implications of a resource adequacy market design on renewable energy systems and energy storage. We discovered that capacity weights, which determine the representation of various power generation technologies in resource adequacy certificates, play a crucial role. If capacity weights are set too low for renewable energy systems and energy storage, which can provide non-energizing capacity, certificates become less appealing, leading to lower system costs, increased renewable energy penetration, and reduced battery degradation. However, if capacity weights are set too high, certificates become more desirable, but this leads to increased battery degradation. A medium-weight approach appears to strike a balance by minimizing battery degradation and maintaining reasonable power costs. Furthermore, our analysis suggests that a resource adequacy certificate value of 0.5-$0.6 per MWh is a suitable starting point for implementation. In this research, a novel approach is proposed to mitigate the object classification-consensus deficit. Finally, we note that the set of representable functions with a finite range, where the range is a countable set, is also countable, but if the range is permitted to be arbitrary, we find that the set of representable functions becomes decidable.  This contrasts with the set of representable reals, which remains undecidable regardless of the condition.  Ultimately, our results highlight the significance of controlling complexity in representations of computable objects. Few-shot instance segmentation is a complex computer vision task that involves identifying and labeling distinct objects within images using only a few examples. It's an important application with various practical uses, such as in image and video processing. 

The foundation of few-shot instance segmentation relies on semantic segmentation, and one way to achieve this is by using support images to train instance segmentation models. However, relying solely on support images can result in poor performance and limitations. For instance, support images may not accurately represent the target scene due to differences in lighting, weather, or other factors. To address this issue, we propose a new approach called PREDICT. It involves predicting potential distractions in the query image using features extracted from support images. 

Another challenge in few-shot instance segmentation is dealing with complex backgrounds. To address this, we developed an iterative strategy that eliminates unnecessary pixels, focusing on pixels with high object-to-background contrast. Our approach uses a weighted loss function to update the model, and the weights are calculated based on the relative frequency of class labels in the dataset. 

Our proposed methods were tested on the Waymo open dataset, and the results show that PREDICT improves the state-of-the-art performance by 7.1% in terms of mean average precision. To identify individuals with dilated airways who do not have a known condition causing them, we used a CT scan database to develop a new classification system.  Our goal was to identify patients with abnormal airway dilatation and create a new condition called Generalized Airway Dilatation (GAD).  By applying a combination of deep learning techniques, including hierarchical clustering and convolutional neural networks, we were able to identify regions of dilatation and create a map of affected airways down to the level of small bronchi. Additionally, we found that patients with GAD have normal lung function but abnormal airway function, and their airway dilatation is more widespread than typically expected.  Our study suggests that GAD could be an underdiagnosed condition that may share similarities with bronchiectasis.  Our new classification system for GAD using deep learning is a significant contribution to the field, and further research is necessary to understand the pathophysiology of GAD. To efficiently handle these maps in real-time, acquiring an accurate lighting solution is crucial. The problem lies in that real-time lighting maps often feature ambiguous illumination data, making direct reproduction impossible. This paper proposes a novel lighting model that circumvents these limitations by leveraging the simplifying effects of overcast environments. The proposed solution, Overcast Lighting Map, achieves a balance between authentic illumination and ease of acquisition, rendering scenes in real-time with high visual fidelity. The model's data density is optimized for real-time performance, and its domain is defined through observations of overcast weather patterns. The resulting rendering technique produces a unique aesthetic that can be applied across a range of genres, from realistic to stylized visual effects. The performance and accuracy of the OLMap have been validated through user studies, demonstrating its ability to produce high-quality results in both photorealistic and stylized contexts.
